notes.definition: Chromatography is a method used to separate the substances in a mixture and help identify them. It has a stationary phase and a mobile phase; substances separate because each one is distributed differently between the two phases, so they move different distances.
explanation: All chromatography uses two phases. The stationary phase does not move: in paper chromatography it is the paper. The mobile phase moves through the stationary phase: in paper chromatography it is the solvent (for example water or ethanol), which soaks up the paper. As the solvent moves, it carries the substances in the mixture with it.

Separation depends on how each substance is distributed between the two phases. A substance that is very soluble in the solvent and only weakly attracted to the paper spends more of its time in the mobile phase, so it moves a long way up the paper. A substance that is more strongly attracted to the paper, or less soluble in the solvent, spends more time in the stationary phase and moves a shorter distance. A substance that is insoluble in the solvent stays on the start line.

In required practical 6, a pencil line is drawn about 1 to 2 cm above the bottom of a sheet of chromatography paper. Small, concentrated spots of each ink or food colouring are placed on the line. The paper is put in a beaker with solvent below the pencil line, and a lid is placed on top. When the solvent has nearly reached the top, the paper is removed and the solvent front is marked in pencil. The dried paper is called a chromatogram.

Each spot can be described by its Rf value: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. Both distances are measured from the start line, to the centre of the spot and to the solvent front. Rf has no units and is always less than 1. A compound has a specific Rf value in a particular solvent, but it has different Rf values in different solvents. Unknown substances can be identified by comparing their Rf values with those of known reference substances run in the same solvent.

A pure compound gives a single spot in all solvents. A mixture may separate into two or more spots, although two substances could have the same Rf value in one solvent, so it is good practice to repeat in a different solvent. If an unknown spot matches a reference spot in Rf value (and colour) in several solvents, it is very likely to be the same substance. Chromatography is used to check food colourings, analyse inks in forensic work, and test the purity of medicines.
keyFacts: Chromatography separates mixtures and helps identify substances.
Stationary phase: the paper (does not move). Mobile phase: the solvent (moves).
Separation depends on how each substance is distributed between the mobile and stationary phases.
Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
Rf has no units and is always between 0 and 1.
A compound has different Rf values in different solvents.
A pure compound produces a single spot in all solvents.
Draw the start line in pencil, not ink, because pencil does not dissolve in the solvent.
The solvent level must be below the start line, or the spots would dissolve into the solvent.
A lid stops the solvent evaporating, so the air inside stays saturated with solvent vapour.

keyTerms.definition: A technique that separates the substances in a mixture using a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
The phase that does not move; in paper chromatography, the paper.
The phase that moves through the stationary phase; in paper chromatography, the solvent.
The furthest point reached by the solvent as it moves up the paper.
Distance moved by a substance divided by distance moved by the solvent, both measured from the start line.
The pattern of spots produced on the paper after chromatography.
The pencil line on which the samples are spotted at the beginning.

equations.name: Rf value
equations.formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
equations.symbols: Rf = distance to centre of spot ÷ distance to solvent front

workedExamples.title: Calculating an Rf value
workedExamples.question: On a chromatogram, the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the start line. A red spot is 3.6 cm from the start line. Calculate the Rf value of the red substance.
steps: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.

workedExamples.title: Measuring from the start line
workedExamples.question: The start line is 1.5 cm from the bottom of the paper. The centre of a blue spot is 6.3 cm from the bottom and the solvent front is 11.5 cm from the bottom. Calculate the Rf value.
steps: Distances must be measured from the start line, not the bottom of the paper.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging the Rf equation
workedExamples.question: A dye has an Rf value of 0.65 in water. The solvent front moves 9.2 cm from the start line. How far does the dye move?
steps: Distance moved by substance = Rf × distance moved by solvent.
= 5.98 cm, which is 6.0 cm to 2 significant figures.

workedExamples.title: Identifying a dye
workedExamples.question: An unknown food colouring X gives two spots with Rf values 0.32 and 0.71. Reference dyes have Rf values: E102 0.71, E110 0.55, E133 0.32, E124 0.48 in the same solvent. Which dyes are in X?
steps: Compare each Rf value for X with the reference values measured in the same solvent.
X gives two spots, so it is a mixture of these two dyes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw the start line in ink or felt-tip pen.
misconceptions.right: In fact the start line must be in pencil; ink would dissolve in the solvent and run up the paper, confusing the results. Graphite is insoluble.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often measure distances from the bottom edge of the paper.
misconceptions.right: In fact both distances are measured from the start line: to the centre of the spot and to the solvent front.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Rf = distance moved by solvent ÷ distance moved by substance, giving values bigger than 1.
misconceptions.right: In fact Rf = substance ÷ solvent, so it is always less than 1 because the substance never moves further than the solvent.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think one spot in one solvent proves a substance is pure.
misconceptions.right: In fact two substances could have the same Rf in one solvent. A pure compound gives a single spot in all solvents, so test in more than one solvent.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a substance that stays on the start line has not been tested properly.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is insoluble in that solvent; try a different solvent.

realWorld: Food scientists use chromatography to check that only permitted food colourings are present in sweets and drinks.
Forensic scientists compare the inks in a forged document or ransom note with inks from suspects' pens.
Pharmaceutical companies use chromatography to check drugs for impurities.
Chromatography is used to test athletes' urine for banned substances.
examTips: Learn the reasons for each step: pencil line (does not dissolve), solvent below the line (spots would dissolve into the solvent), lid (stops solvent evaporating), small concentrated spots (clear separation).
Always measure Rf distances from the start line to the centre of the spot. Give Rf as a decimal with no units.
If a question asks how to tell if a substance is pure, say 'a pure substance gives one spot in all solvents'.
To identify a substance, compare Rf values with reference substances run in the same solvent (and ideally on the same paper).
In 'explain the separation' questions, use the phrase 'distributed between the mobile and stationary phases'.
summary: Paper chromatography: paper is the stationary phase, solvent is the mobile phase.
Substances separate because they distribute differently between the two phases.
Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
Rf values depend on the solvent; compare with references in the same solvent.
Pure compounds give one spot in every solvent; mixtures may give several.
Use a pencil start line above the solvent level, and a lid.

questions.question: In paper chromatography, what is the stationary phase?
options: The solvent
The paper
The pencil line
The ink
markScheme: 1 mark: The paper
questions.explanation: The paper does not move, so it is the stationary phase. The solvent is the mobile phase.

questions.question: Which equation is used to calculate an Rf value?
options: Rf = distance moved by solvent ÷ distance moved by substance
Rf = distance moved by solvent − distance moved by substance
Rf = distance moved by substance × distance moved by solvent
Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
markScheme: 1 mark: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
questions.explanation: Rf is the substance distance divided by the solvent distance, so it is always less than 1.

questions.question: Why is the start line on chromatography paper drawn in pencil?
options: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent
Pencil is easier to see
Pencil helps the solvent move up the paper
Ink would react with the paper
markScheme: 1 mark: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent
questions.explanation: Graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so the line stays where it is. Ink would dissolve and run up the paper with the samples.

questions.question: How many spots does a pure compound produce on a chromatogram?
options: None
Two
One
One for each element in the compound
markScheme: 1 mark: One
questions.explanation: A pure compound gives a single spot in all solvents. A common error is to think a compound separates into its elements: chromatography separates substances in mixtures, it does not break compounds down.

questions.question: Why must the solvent level be below the start line?
options: So that the paper does not tear
So that the spots do not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker
So that the solvent moves faster
So that the Rf values are larger
markScheme: 1 mark: So that the spots do not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker
questions.explanation: If the spots were under the solvent, they would wash into the solvent in the beaker instead of being carried up the paper.

questions.question:
A student uses paper chromatography to separate an ink, using water as the solvent.
Figure 1 shows the chromatogram.
The ink stays on the start line.
Which is the best explanation?
options: The ink is pure
The paper was too wet
The ink has an Rf value of 1
The ink is insoluble in water
markScheme: 1 mark: The ink is insoluble in water
questions.explanation: A substance that does not dissolve in the mobile phase is not carried up the paper, so its Rf is 0 in that solvent. A different solvent should be tried.

questions.question: Why is a lid placed on the beaker during paper chromatography?
options: To stop the solvent evaporating
To keep light out
To stop the spots fading
To keep the paper dry
markScheme: 1 mark: To stop the solvent evaporating
questions.explanation: A lid keeps the atmosphere in the beaker saturated with solvent vapour, so solvent does not evaporate from the paper before reaching the top.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram of two substances, A and B, in the same solvent.
Substance A travels further up the paper than substance B.
Which statement explains this?
options: A is more strongly attracted to the paper than B
A is less soluble in the solvent than B
A spends more of its time in the mobile phase than B
A has a larger Rf value because it is a heavier molecule
markScheme: 1 mark: A spends more of its time in the mobile phase than B
questions.explanation: A substance that is distributed more into the mobile phase (more soluble in the solvent, less attracted to the paper) moves further. Molecule mass is not the explanation at GCSE.

questions.question: A sample gives one spot with Rf = 0.40 in water. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: The sample is definitely pure
The sample may be pure; it should be tested in a different solvent
The sample is definitely a mixture
The sample is insoluble in water
markScheme: 1 mark: The sample may be pure; it should be tested in a different solvent
questions.explanation: Two substances can have the same Rf in one solvent. A pure compound gives one spot in all solvents, so further solvents are needed before concluding it is pure.

questions.question: Which of these Rf values cannot be correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.25
questions.explanation: Rf can never be more than 1 because a substance cannot travel further than the solvent front.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram of a dye.
Calculate the Rf value of the dye.
Use the equation:
Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.40
questions.explanation: Rf = substance ÷ solvent = 3.0 ÷ 7.5 = 0.40. Rf has no units.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram of a green food colouring.
Calculate the Rf value of the green substance.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.30
questions.explanation: Rf = 2.1 ÷ 7.0 = 0.30. Dividing the other way round gives 3.33, which is impossible for an Rf value.

questions.question:
A substance has an Rf value of 0.65 in ethanol.
The solvent front moves 9.2 cm from the start line.
Calculate the distance moved by the substance from the start line.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: distance = 0.65 × 9.2
questions.explanation: Rearrange Rf = substance ÷ solvent to give substance = Rf × solvent = 0.65 × 9.2 = 5.98 cm = 6.0 cm.

questions.question:
A student measured the distances on a chromatogram from the bottom edge of the paper instead of from the start line.
Table 1 shows the student's measurements.
Calculate the correct Rf value of the substance.
markScheme: 1 mark: substance distance = 6.3 − 1.5 = 4.8 cm
1 mark: solvent distance = 11.5 − 1.5 = 10.0 cm
questions.explanation: Distances must be from the start line. Using 6.3 ÷ 11.5 = 0.55 is a common error.

headers: Distance from bottom edge of paper in cm

questions.question:
A dye has an Rf value of 0.40.
The dye moves 3.0 cm from the start line.
Calculate the distance moved by the solvent from the start line.
markScheme: 1 mark: solvent distance = 3.0 ÷ 0.40
1 mark: 7.5 cm
questions.explanation: Rearrange: solvent distance = substance distance ÷ Rf = 3.0 ÷ 0.40 = 7.5 cm.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram of a dye.
The distances have been measured in different units.
Calculate the Rf value of the dye.
markScheme: 1 mark: convert to same units: 70 mm = 7.0 cm (or 4.2 cm = 42 mm)
questions.explanation: Both distances must be in the same units before dividing. 42 ÷ 70 = 0.60.

questions.question: Name the mobile phase and the stationary phase in paper chromatography.
markScheme: 1 mark: mobile phase is the solvent
1 mark: stationary phase is the paper
questions.explanation: The solvent moves through the paper, carrying the substances.

questions.question: Explain how paper chromatography separates the dyes in an ink.
acceptedAnswers: dyes distributed between mobile and stationary phases
markScheme: 1 mark: the solvent (mobile phase) moves up the paper and carries the dyes
1 mark: each dye is distributed differently between the mobile and stationary phases (different solubility / attraction to paper), so they move different distances
questions.explanation: More soluble dyes, less attracted to the paper, move further; this spreads the dyes into separate spots.

questions.question: A student puts large spots of ink on the start line. Suggest why small, concentrated spots give better results.
markScheme: 1 mark: large spots spread out / overlap with each other
1 mark: small spots give clearer, separate spots so Rf values can be measured accurately
questions.explanation: Small spots (applied several times and dried in between to concentrate them) separate cleanly.

questions.question: Describe how a student can use paper chromatography to show whether a brown food colouring contains a dye called E110. Reference samples are available.
acceptedAnswers: spot brown colouring and E110 on start line
markScheme: 1 mark: put spots of the brown colouring and of E110 on the same pencil start line
1 mark: place in solvent (below the line) and allow solvent to move up the paper
1 mark: if the brown colouring has a spot at the same height / same Rf value (and colour) as E110, it contains E110
questions.explanation: Running the reference on the same paper in the same solvent gives a fair comparison.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the Rf values of a dye in two different solvents.
Explain why the Rf values are different.
markScheme: 1 mark: the dye has a different solubility in each solvent / its distribution between the mobile and stationary phases depends on the solvent
1 mark: it is more soluble in water (spends more time in the mobile phase), so it moves further in water
questions.explanation: Rf values are specific to a substance in a particular solvent, so reference values must use the same solvent.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram.
Give the name of line X.
markScheme: 1 mark: solvent front
questions.explanation: It is marked in pencil as soon as the paper is removed, before the solvent evaporates.

questions.question: A student forgets to mark the solvent front before the paper dries. Explain why this is a problem.
markScheme: 1 mark: the solvent evaporates so the front can no longer be seen
1 mark: so the distance moved by the solvent is unknown and Rf values cannot be calculated
questions.explanation: The solvent front must be marked immediately, because Rf needs the solvent distance.

questions.question: Describe how a student could carry out paper chromatography to separate the dyes in a black felt-tip pen ink.
markScheme: Indicative content: draw a start line in pencil about 1 to 2 cm from the bottom of the paper
Put a small spot of ink on the line
Pour solvent (for example water) into a beaker to a depth below the start line
Hang/stand the paper in the beaker with the bottom edge in the solvent
Put a lid on the beaker
Leave until the solvent has nearly reached the top
Remove the paper and mark the solvent front in pencil; let it dry
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear, logical method including pencil line, solvent below line and allowing solvent to rise
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps but missing key details
questions.explanation: Key credit-worthy points are the pencil line, the solvent level below the line and allowing the solvent to move up the paper.

questions.question:
A student wants to find out which dyes are in an orange drink. Four reference dyes, A, B, C and D, are available.
Describe a method the student could use, and explain how the student would analyse the chromatogram to identify the dyes, including how Rf values would be used and how the student could be confident of the identification.
markScheme: Indicative content: pencil start line near the bottom of chromatography paper
Small concentrated spots of the drink and of each reference dye A to D, spaced along the line
Place in a beaker of solvent with the solvent below the start line; use a lid
Remove when solvent near the top; mark solvent front; dry
Compare the spots from the drink with the reference spots: same height/colour means same dye
Measure distance from start line to centre of each spot and to solvent front
Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
Matching Rf values (in the same solvent) identify the dyes
Number of spots from the drink shows how many dyes (at least) it contains
Any spot that matches no reference is an unknown dye
Repeat with a different solvent: matching Rf values in more than one solvent gives more confidence, since two dyes could share an Rf in one solvent
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, logical method and full analysis using Rf values, including the need for the same solvent and confirmation in another solvent
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): workable method and some analysis, for example comparing positions of spots or calculating Rf
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic relevant statements about spotting and solvent
questions.explanation: Top answers combine a correct method with clear use of Rf values and an explanation of why testing in a second solvent increases confidence.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chromatogram of ink X.
What does the chromatogram show about ink X?
options: X is a pure substance
X contains at least three different substances
X contains exactly three elements
X is insoluble in the solvent
markScheme: 1 mark: X contains at least three different substances
questions.explanation: Each separate spot is a different substance, so X is a mixture of at least three substances (some could overlap or stay on the line).

questions.question: What should be put on the beaker to stop the solvent evaporating?
options: A thermometer
A filter funnel
A lid
A Bunsen burner
markScheme: 1 mark: A lid
questions.explanation: A lid (or watch glass) traps the solvent vapour.
